questions.text: Why should implicit skill routing filter by invocation eligibility before ranking relevance?

options.A: So the highest relevance score automatically grants permission to activate.
options.B: So all discovered skills enter context before policy is evaluated.
options.C: So a blocked top match does not hide an eligible lower-scoring alternative.
options.D: So explicit user invocation can bypass the host’s permission policy.

questions.explanation: Eligibility defines the candidate set, then relevance ranks permitted candidates. Ranking first and stopping after a blocked winner can miss a valid alternative.

questions.text: You evaluate a release-readiness skill. Which test best probes its near-miss routing boundary?

options.A: A request to inspect a prepared version before publishing.
options.B: A request asking why today’s package build failed.
options.C: An unrelated question about rotary position embeddings.

questions.explanation: A build failure shares release-related vocabulary but belongs to a different workflow, making it a useful near miss.

questions.text: In route_request’s explicit-human branch, the named skill exists but adapter.allows returns False. The decision records selected.name and score=1.0. Does it allow activation?

options.A: Yes, because exact-name selection always overrides eligibility.
options.B: Yes, because score=1.0 is sufficient evidence of completion.
options.C: No, because an explicit name is ignored for human callers.
options.D: No, because the returned decision’s allowed field is False despite the exact match.

questions.explanation: The explicit branch preserves selection identity and score but uses adapter.allows for the allowed field. Exact selection does not bypass policy.
